gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 45 W charger under $20 loses watts under sustained load: smartzone.de (Jan, 2 Aug 2026) measured the UGREEN Nexode Air 45W dropping from 45 W to 40 W after exactly 30 minutes at 22 °C (25 W on a larger battery), with a PPS ceiling of 11 V and a 71 °C housing. Notebookcheck measured the Nexode Air Slim 45W at 43.52 W peak and 38.30 W after about 47 minutes.
standout_why: Compared against the cited TechGearLab Anker Nano 30W review (29.4 W measured max, iPhone 17 Pro 10→60% in 29 min, no temperature figure) and the cited Android Authority best-USB-C list (Nano 3 30W: 27 W over PPS, 89.3% efficiency, 74 g; no 45 W sub-$20 charger measured). The cited Tom's Hardware best-chargers page and its uncited 20-charger test would not render in the fetcher, so their figures could not be checked. None of the pages read measures how a 45 W sub-$20 charger holds up over time, its PPS voltage ceiling, or its temperature.
decides: This confirms the cluster map's 45 W tier but qualifies it. The UGREEN Nexode Air 45W's headline 45 W is a starting figure (40 W after 30 min, per smartzone.de), and its 5–11 V PPS window cannot supply the 20 V/3 A PPS mode the cluster rules cite for the Galaxy S26 Ultra. The Anker Nano Charger Neo's 65 W peak is real on a Mac (The Gadgeteer read 59.8 W in macOS), but AVS was not negotiated there, and Anker says output drops after about 20 minutes at 65 W. No under-$20 charger has a named AVS measurement on an iPhone 18 Pro. For a 30 W phone-only buyer, the Anker Nano 3 30W stays the measured pick (rivals already print its 29.4 W).
